title: Minimal POS: Group the Zeros and Read the Sum Terms
quickIdea: To get a minimal product of sums, group the 0s exactly as you would group 1s, then read each group as a sum term with the polarity inverted.
remember: A minimal POS is the minimal cover of the complement: group the 0s of F, and each group becomes one sum term (one factor).
Read the sum term with inverted polarity: a variable that is 0 across the group appears plain, a variable that is 1 across the group appears complemented. For a group of 1s it is the other way round.
The group rules are unchanged: power-of-two rectangles, wrap-around allowed, largest groups first, overlap allowed, every 0 covered at least once.
Equivalently, minimise F' as an SOP and apply De Morgan: F' = B'D' + BD becomes F = (B + D)(B' + D').
Don't cares may be grouped with the 0s when that enlarges a group, exactly as they may be grouped with the 1s for an SOP.
A minimal SOP and a minimal POS of the same function need not cost the same; when the question fixes the form, minimise in that form only.

example.prompt: Find the minimal POS of f(w,x,y,z) = Sigma m(0, 1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 10) + Sigma d(5, 6, 11, 15).
example.work: The 0s are 4, 9, 12, 13, 14. Group them: {4, 6, 12, 14} uses the don't cares at 6 and 14 and gives x = 1, z = 0 throughout, so the factor is (x' + z). {9, 11, 13, 15} uses the don't cares at 11 and 15 and gives w = 1, z = 1, so the factor is (w' + z'). Every 0 is covered: 4, 12 and 14 by the first group, 9 and 13 by the second.
example.answer: f = (x' + z)(w' + z'), two factors and four literals - the minimal POS.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2017 Set 2 Q.28 asks for the minimum POS of a function given as minterms plus don't cares, and all four options are two-factor products, so the whole question is whether you grouped the 0s or the 1s. GATE CSE 2015 Set 3 Q.44 tests the same idea from the notation side, by asking whether a Pi M list matches a given function.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2017 Set 2 Q.28: f(w,x,y,z) = Sigma m(0,1,2,3,7,8,10) + Sigma d(5,6,11,15). Which is a minimum POS form? (A) (w' + z')(x' + z)  (B) (w' + z)(x + z)  (C) (w + z)(x' + z)  (D) (w + z')(x' + z)
variations.why: Grouping the zeros with the don't cares gives {4,6,12,14} = (x' + z) and {9,11,13,15} = (w' + z'). Checking the other options on the rows that decide it: at w = 0, x = 0, y = 0, z = 0 (a required 1, m0) option (B) gives (w' + z) = 1 and (x + z) = 0, so its product is 0 and it is not equivalent; the same test rules out (C) and (D).

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: F has 0s at 0, 2, 5 and 7 in a three-variable map. Write its minimal POS and its minimal SOP.
variations.answer: POS: F = (A + C)(A' + C'). SOP: F = A'C + AC'.
variations.why: The 0s {0,2} have A = 0 and C = 0, so the factor is (A + C); the 0s {5,7} have A = 1 and C = 1, so the factor is (A' + C'). The 1s are 1, 3, 4 and 6, which group as {1,3} = A'C and {4,6} = AC'. Both forms come to two 2-literal terms - here the two forms tie, which is not the general case.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: Given F = Pi M(0, 1, 2, 3, 4), find the minimal POS in a three-variable map.
variations.why: The 0s are rows 0 to 4, which is A = 0 together with row 4 (100). The group of 0s at 0,1,2,3 gives the factor (A); minterm 4 is a 1 so it is not grouped. Hence F = A - one literal, and its SOP form is A as well.

trap.what: Reading a sum term with the same polarity as a product term.
trap.why: A product term describes where a group of 1s is 1; a sum term describes where a group of 0s is 0. The variable that is 0 in the group must appear plain in the sum, which is the opposite of the product-term rule.
trap.counterexample: For the group of 0s {0, 2} in a three-variable map, both cells have A = 0 and C = 0, so the factor is (A + C), not (A' + C'). Expanding (A' + C') instead gives the complement's factor.

check.question: F(w,x,y,z) has 0s at 0, 1, 2, 3 only. Give its minimal POS and its minimal SOP.
check.answer: Both are F = w + x: the POS is the single factor (w + x) and the SOP is the single term w + x.
check.explanation: The 0s at 0, 1, 2 and 3 all have w = 0 and x = 0, so the group of zeros gives the factor (w + x). The 1s are rows 4 to 15, which group as {4,5,6,7} = w'x and {8..15} = w, and w + w'x = w + x. Here the two forms coincide; the worked example above is the case where they do not.

sources.note: read from the opening to the two-variable map, plus the closing summary: truth table to grid, minterm numbering, AB' + AB = A as the first grouping, and the summary's rules - SOP covers every 1 with the fewest and largest power-of-two groups, POS covers the 0s, and a don't care is taken as 0 or 1 according to which makes the group larger. The middle of the served transcript is missing, so no 3- or 4-variable worked example is attributed to it.

sources.note: read the K Map, Min Sum of Products Form and Min Products of Sum Form sections: grouping rules, prime and essential prime implicant definitions, the don't-care rule, the three-step minimal-SOP algorithm (circle the PIs, take every EPI, then the smallest subset that covers the rest) and the POS derivation from the zeros.

sources.title: Karnaugh map: Gray-code ordering, grouping and wrap-around
sources.note: read the construction, grouping and solution sections: Gray-code ordering so neighbours differ in one variable, power-of-two rectangles that may overlap, toroidal connectivity for wrap-around, the reading rule (keep the variables constant across the box, drop the rest), don't cares that may be included in a group or left out, and the POS form obtained by minimising the complement and applying De Morgan.

sourceLine: The POS rule (cover the 0s, and a don't care may join a group of 0s): NPTEL IIT Kharagpur Digital Electronic Circuits Lecture 10 closing summary (English) and GATE Overflow's Digital Logic subject notes (English). The inverted reading of a sum term and the De Morgan route from the complement: the Wikipedia Karnaugh map article (English, read in part). Both forms of the worked example are recomputed in scripts/validate.py.
